title: The Title Was Never the Point 2026
author: Josh Gratsch
summary: Josh Gratsch recounts reaching the CEO role at 31 and feeling nothing a week later. He uses the experience to describe the arrival fallacy, the belief that attaining a title or status will finally make us feel enough. The extraordinary quickly becomes ordinary and the mind moves to the next rung, even when no rung remains. Rather than abandoning ambition, he proposes periodically asking why the goal matters, what gives energy, and which problems and people feel meaningful. Ambition lasts longer when anchored in purpose that outlasts any single goal. For him that purpose is helping others see they are more capable than they believe, and he notes that focusing on it also served the team, product, and business results. The short essay is a candid prompt for leaders to separate the role from the reason they want it.
points: The arrival fallacy is the belief that reaching a title will change how we feel, and it tends to be unteachable until experienced firsthand.
Attaining a goal brings only a fleeting moment of satisfaction before the mind jumps to whatever comes next.
The remedy is not to drop ambition but to ask regularly why you pursue a goal, what energises you, and what strengths and people you want around you.
Purpose that extends beyond one goal makes ambition sustainable, while chasing accomplishment to fill a void leads to disappointment.
The author found his purpose in helping others see they are more capable than they believe, and focusing on it improved team and business outcomes.
quotes: I spent years chasing the CEO position. At 31, I achieved it—and felt nothing a week later.
But eventually, the extraordinary becomes our ordinary. We reach the goal, enjoy it for a fleeting moment, and then our mind jumps to whatever comes next.
That’s the arrival fallacy, and it’s nearly impossible to accept until we experience it firsthand; one of those unteachable lessons.
Without a genuine purpose, we can spend years chasing something, climbing the ladder, only to realize it was never the point.
Ambition becomes more sustainable when it’s grounded in meaning that goes beyond a single goal and reflects everything we do and who we are while doing it.

My purpose as a leader is to help others see they are more capable than they believe. What’s interesting is the more I focus on that, the more it supports what I’m trying to accomplish from a team, product, and business standpoint.
Don’t ever stop pursuing; just be very clear on why you’re doing it.
